name: Spondylolisthesis
populations: adolescent athletes in extension-and-rotation sports (isthmic, usually L5 on S1)
older adults (degenerative, usually L4 on L5)
summary: Forward slip of one lumbar vertebra on the one below: isthmic (pars defect, usually L5 on S1, often adolescent athletes) or degenerative (usually L4 on L5, older adults). Most slips are low grade and benign.

keyFacts.label: Natural history
keyFacts.value: In a 45-year prospective study, unilateral defects never slipped, slip progression slowed each decade and no one reached a 40% slip

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Spondylolysis 5.9% on CT in Japan, 90.3% at L5; a slip was present in 74.5% of bilateral and 7.7% of unilateral defects

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Step-deformity palpation: sensitivity 60–88%, specificity 87–100% for spondylolisthesis in athletes (one low-risk-of-bias study)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Standing lateral radiograph to measure and grade the slip; flexion–extension views for instability; MRI if neural compression is suspected

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Isthmic slips begin in childhood or adolescence, most progressing around the growth spurt; degenerative slips occur in older adults

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most low-grade slips are managed without surgery; surgery helps selected people with persistent disabling symptoms (SPORT as-treated analysis)

overview:
Spondylolisthesis is forward slippage of one vertebra on the vertebra below. The two common types are isthmic spondylolisthesis, in which a defect of the pars interarticularis (spondylolysis) lets the vertebra slip, usually L5 on S1 and often beginning in adolescence, and degenerative spondylolisthesis, in which facet and disc degeneration allow a slip, usually at L4–5 in older adults (clinical teaching). A classification by cause and anatomy dates to Wiltse and colleagues [r1], and the amount of slip is graded by the Meyerding system [r2].

Most slips are low grade and benign. In a CT series of 2000 people, spondylolysis was found in 5.9%, and 90.3% of affected vertebrae were at L5. A slip was present in 74.5% of people with bilateral defects but 7.7% of those with unilateral defects, 60.5% of vertebrae with spondylolysis showed Meyerding grade I or II and none was high grade [r3]. In a 45-year prospective study of people with pars defects who were unselected for pain, the clinical course resembled that of the general population, slip progression slowed with each decade and no one reached a 40% slip [r4]. Most of the slip had already occurred by the first examination in a long-term series of children and adolescents [r5].

Most people are managed without surgery, with education, activity and exercise. Surgery is considered for persistent disabling symptoms, neurological deficit and high-grade slips. In a randomised trial of adults with isthmic slips, fusion improved function and pain more than an exercise program [r6], and in degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis, an as-treated analysis favoured surgery while the randomised comparison was limited by crossover [r7,r8]. The evidence is mostly observational and the decision is a shared one.

epidemiology.text: In a CT review of 2000 people aged 20–92 years who had abdominal or pelvic CT for reasons unrelated to back pain, lumbar spondylolysis was found in 117 (5.9%), at a male-to-female ratio of 2:1. Of 124 affected vertebrae, 112 (90.3%) were at L5 and 21.0% were unilateral. Spina bifida occulta was associated with spondylolysis (odds ratio 3.7). Spondylolisthesis was found in 74.5% of people with bilateral spondylolysis and 7.7% with unilateral spondylolysis, and 75 of 124 vertebrae (60.5%) with spondylolysis showed low-grade (Meyerding I or II) slip with no high-grade slip [r3]. In the Framingham community CT sample, degenerative spondylolisthesis affected 23 of 188 participants (15 female, mean age 62.0 years) [r9]. In a 45-year prospective study that began with 500 first-grade children, 30 individuals were identified with pars lesions [r4].

intrinsic: Bilateral pars defects: slip was found in 74.5% of bilateral defects versus 7.7% of unilateral defects [r3]
Spina bifida occulta (odds ratio 3.7 for spondylolysis) and male sex (2:1) for the pars defect itself [r3]
The growth spurt: slips tended to progress in the age groups corresponding to early puberty (girls 9–12, boys 11–14 years) [r5]
The percentage of the initial slip, the only radiological variable that predicted progression in children and adolescents [r5]
For degenerative slips: older age, sex and severe facet joint osteoarthritis were associated, while disc narrowing was not [r9]
extrinsic: Sports with repeated lumbar extension and rotation under load (gymnastics, diving, fast bowling, throwing, rowing), the usual setting for the pars stress fracture that precedes isthmic slip (clinical teaching; see the spondylolysis page)
Heavy repetitive loading in adulthood (plausible association for degenerative slips; not tested in the sources reviewed)

mechanism.summary: In the isthmic type, repeated extension and rotation load the pars interarticularis until it fails as a stress fracture. When the defect does not unite on both sides, nothing links the vertebral body to its posterior arch, so the body and the superior part of the arch are free to slide forward on the segment below under anterior shear, most often L5 on S1 [r3]. In the degenerative type there is no pars defect: facet joint osteoarthritis and disc degeneration let the vertebra slip forward, usually at L4–5 (clinical teaching), and facet osteoarthritis was strongly associated with it [r9].
sequence: In a growing athlete, repeated lumbar extension and rotation load the pars interarticularis of L5 (the usual site) [r3].
Microdamage accumulates faster than the pars can repair itself, and a stress reaction develops, then a fracture (see the spondylolysis page).
If the defect fails to unite on both sides, the L5 vertebral body is disconnected from its posterior elements [r3].
Anterior shear forces on the lumbosacral junction (upright posture, extension, sport) push the L5 body forward on S1.
The slip occurs mostly early; 90% of the final slip had already occurred at the first radiological examination in a long-term series of 272 children and adolescents [r5].

The disc beneath the slipped level degenerates and loses height, and the fibrocartilage at the pars defect and the bulging disc can narrow the foramen and compress the exiting root (clinical teaching).
In the degenerative type, facet osteoarthritis and ligament and disc degeneration allow forward translation at L4–5 in older adults, with stenosis and neurogenic claudication [r9,r7].

variants.name: Isthmic spondylolisthesis (Wiltse type II)
variants.description: A pars defect (lytic) or elongation (stretched pars) allows the slip. It usually begins in childhood or adolescence, at L5–S1, and was found in 74.5% of bilateral pars defects [r1,r3].

variants.name: Degenerative spondylolisthesis (Wiltse type III)
variants.description: Intersegmental degeneration without a pars defect, in older adults, usually at L4–5. Severe facet osteoarthritis was found at 20 of 24 slipped segments in a community sample, and disc narrowing was not independently associated [r1,r9].

variants.name: Dysplastic spondylolisthesis (Wiltse type I)
variants.description: Congenital dysplasia of the upper sacrum or L5 arch lets L5 slip without a primary fracture, with a higher risk of progression to high-grade slip [r1,r10].

variants.name: Traumatic and pathological types (Wiltse types IV and V)
variants.description: Acute fracture of the posterior elements, or bone disease such as tumour or infection, weaken the restraints to slip. They are uncommon and are part of the differential diagnosis [r1].

variants.name: Progression in a growing athlete
variants.description: In 86 young athletes with spondylolysis or spondylolisthesis, displacement increased in 33 (average 10.5%) over 4.8 years of training, did not progress in 36 and decreased in 7; all were asymptomatic throughout [r11].

anatomy.text: Each lumbar vertebra is linked to the one below by the disc in front and by two facet joints behind. The pars interarticularis is the narrow isthmus of the posterior arch between the superior and inferior articular processes, and it carries the shear load that resists forward translation. At the lumbosacral junction the L5 body sits on the sloping upper surface of S1, so gravity and anterior shear push L5 forward, and the facet joints, disc and iliolumbar ligaments resist this. The L5 root travels in the lateral recess behind the L5–S1 disc and exits the foramen under the L5 pedicle, so a slip, the fibrocartilage at a pars defect and a degenerate disc can all narrow the foramen and the L5 root canal. In a degenerative slip the posterior elements are intact and slip forward with the body, narrowing the central canal rather than the foramen.

structures.name: Pars interarticularis
structures.role: The isthmus of the posterior arch between the facets; in isthmic spondylolisthesis it fails (a defect, usually bilateral at L5) [r3]

structures.name: Facet (zygapophyseal) joints
structures.role: Resist forward shear and rotation; their osteoarthritis is strongly associated with degenerative slips [r9]

structures.name: Intervertebral disc (L5–S1, L4–5)
structures.role: Holds the bodies together in front; it degenerates and loses height as the slip progresses (clinical teaching)

structures.name: Nerve roots (L5 in the L5–S1 foramen; the cauda equina centrally)
structures.role: Exiting root compressed at the foramen in isthmic slips (clinical teaching); central stenosis from degenerative slips causes neurogenic claudication

structures.name: Multifidus and deep abdominal muscles
structures.role: Provide dynamic segmental control, and were the target of the specific exercise trial in this condition [r12]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Isthmic spondylolisthesis is the consequence of a pars defect that has not united. Under anterior shear the vertebral body slides forward while the posterior arch (and the facets above) stay with the lower segment, and the amount of slip is graded as a percentage of the vertebral width [r2]. Most of the slip occurs early: 90% of the final slip had already occurred at the first radiological examination in 272 children and adolescents followed for a mean 14.8 years, and the percentage of the primary slip was the only radiological variable that predicted progression [r5]. In a 45-year prospective study, slip progression slowed with each decade and was not associated with low back pain [r4].

Degenerative spondylolisthesis arises from intersegmental degeneration. In a community CT sample, age, sex and facet joint osteoarthritis were associated with the slip, but disc narrowing was not, which does not support the idea that disc degeneration must come first [r9]. Pain does not track the slip: people with pars defects had SF-36 scores similar to the general population [r4], so the slip is only one contributor to symptoms in those who have them, together with instability, foraminal or central narrowing and deconditioning.

structures.name: Pars interarticularis
structures.effect: Bilateral defect (non-union of the pars stress fracture) disconnects the vertebral body from its posterior arch [r3]

structures.name: Facet joints
structures.effect: Osteoarthritis with capsular laxity in degenerative slips; severe osteoarthritis at 20 of 24 slipped segments in a community sample [r9]

structures.name: Intervertebral disc
structures.effect: Loses height and bulges as the slip progresses and shear loading increases (clinical teaching)

structures.name: Exiting nerve root (L5 in L5–S1 slips)
structures.effect: Compressed in the foramen by the displaced body, disc and fibrocartilage at the defect, causing radicular pain (clinical teaching)

structures.name: Central canal and cauda equina (degenerative L4–5 slips)
structures.effect: Narrowed by the slip with facet and ligament hypertrophy, causing neurogenic claudication [r7,r8]

muscles.name: Multifidus and deep abdominal muscles
muscles.effect: Segmental control is a target of treatment: a trial of specific exercise with deep abdominal activation and multifidus co-activation improved pain and disability in chronic spondylolysis or spondylolisthesis [r12]

muscles.name: Erector spinae and hamstrings
muscles.effect: Protective spasm and tight hamstrings are clinically common in symptomatic slips, especially in adolescents (clinical observation; not tested in the sources reviewed)

muscles.name: Hip flexors
muscles.effect: Shortening increases anterior pelvic tilt and lumbar lordosis, which raises shear at the lumbosacral junction (clinical reasoning; not tested in the sources reviewed)

muscles.name: Myotomes of the compressed root (L5, S1)
muscles.effect: Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, great toe extension or plantarflexion if the root is compressed (clinical teaching)

cellular.description: Resorption outpaces formation, microcracks accumulate and a stress fracture develops through the pars (see the spondylolysis page).
A chronic defect fills with fibrous and fibrocartilaginous tissue rather than bone, leaving a mobile gap (clinical teaching).

cellular.timing: Mostly early, around the growth spurt
cellular.description: Most of the displacement occurs by the first radiographic examination, with a tendency to progress during the early pubertal growth spurt [r5].
Disc height loss and facet osteoarthritis follow, and in degenerative slips they allow the slip itself [r9].
Narrowing of the foramen or central canal produces radicular pain or neurogenic claudication, usually in adults [r7].

systems.effect: A lumbosacral step, increased lordosis and pelvic tilt and hamstring tightness are common in symptomatic slips (clinical observation)
Radicular pain from foraminal compression or neurogenic claudication from central narrowing; the L5 root is most often affected in isthmic L5–S1 slips (clinical teaching)

Pain does not simply track the slip: people with pars defects followed a course similar to the general population [r4], and pain sensitisation and fear of movement contribute in people with persistent pain (clinical observation)
Slip progression is concentrated around the early pubertal growth spurt and early after diagnosis; the percentage of initial slip predicts progression [r5]
Fear of activity and restriction from sport can follow the diagnosis; evidence does not justify a blanket sport ban for limited slips [r11]

grades.description: Slip of up to a quarter of the width of the vertebral body. Standard Meyerding convention; the percentage bands are not tied to a cited source here.
grades.prognosis: Low grade: studies suggest a benign course for slips under 50% [r10]. Grades I and II made up 60.5% of vertebrae with spondylolysis on CT [r3]

grades.description: Slip of a quarter to a half of the vertebral width.
grades.prognosis: Low grade; benign course in studies, but many patients still present with pain and activity limitation [r10]

grades.description: Slip of half to three quarters of the vertebral width. High grade.
grades.prognosis: Slip progression is a specific concern in high-grade and dysplastic slips, and surgery is commonly recommended; higher slip angle is associated with failure of non-surgical treatment (Level III) [r10]

grades.description: Slip of three quarters to the full vertebral width. High grade.
grades.prognosis: As for grade III; refer for specialist spinal opinion [r10]

grades.description: The vertebral body has slipped completely off the one below.
grades.prognosis: Specialist surgical management; no high-grade slip was found in the 2000-person CT series [r3]

timeframes.summary: Isthmic slips occur early and then change little: 90% of the final slip had occurred by the first examination in a long-term series [r5], and in a 45-year study slip progression slowed each decade [r4]. Symptom recovery depends on the program; a specific exercise trial ran 10 weeks with benefit maintained at 30 months [r12].

healing.description: Understand the condition, modify provocative loading and start gentle movement (clinical convention)
A 10-week specific exercise program reduced pain and disability in chronic spondylolysis or spondylolisthesis [r12]
Progressive hip, trunk and leg strength and graded return to sport or work (clinical convention)

healing.phase: Monitoring to skeletal maturity or long-term self-management
healing.description: Growing athletes need monitoring around the growth spurt [r5]; adults need a self-management plan; outcomes in trials are reported at 2 to 4 years [r7,r8]

milestones.label: Baseline standing lateral radiograph recorded
milestones.note: Measure the slip percentage and note the slip angle in high-grade slips [r10]

milestones.label: End of a 10-week specific stabilisation program
milestones.note: Pain and disability fell in a randomised trial [r12]

milestones.label: Review of response; refer if disabling symptoms persist
2-year outcomes in the surgical trials
milestones.note: Surgery favoured in the as-treated SPORT analysis [r7]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based. Adolescents with a low-grade, minimally symptomatic slip often continue sport; there is no justification for a blanket ban [r11]. Symptomatic athletes need a graded return when pain-free and with good control, usually 3–6 months, and high-grade slips need specialist advice. No validated criteria were identified; the criteria below are clinical convention.

symptoms: Low back pain, often aggravated by extension, standing and walking, and sometimes by sitting (pain worse with sitting and walking had sensitivity above 75% for spondylolisthesis in athletes) [r13]
Buttock or posterior thigh pain, often unilateral
Leg radicular pain, numbness or weakness (commonly L5) if a root is compressed (clinical teaching)
Neurogenic claudication in older adults with degenerative slips with stenosis: buttock and leg symptoms on walking, relieved by sitting [r7]
A feeling of back instability, or catching on bending and returning upright (clinical observation)
Many slips are asymptomatic: athletes with progressing slips remained asymptomatic [r11]
signs: Palpable step at the slipped spinous process, which had good accuracy in one low-risk-of-bias study of athletes [r13]
Increased lumbar lordosis, a flattened buttock and a prominent sacral or lumbosacral step in higher-grade slips (clinical observation)
Tight hamstrings and a shortened stride (Phalen–Dickson sign) especially in adolescents (clinical observation)
Pain on lumbar extension or sustained standing, easing with flexion
Neurological signs (reduced ankle reflex, L5 or S1 weakness or sensory loss) in a minority

subjective: Age, sport and training volume, especially extension-and-rotation sports and the timing of the growth spurt [r5]
Pain site, behaviour with extension, standing, walking and sitting [r13]
Leg symptoms: distribution, radicular or claudication pattern, and the effect of sitting and bending forward
Neurological and sphincter symptoms: leg weakness, saddle numbness, bladder, bowel and sexual function
Previous imaging, bracing or treatment, and family history of pars defects or spondylolisthesis
Function and goals: sport, work, walking tolerance, sleep and mood
observation: Increased lordosis, flat buttock, prominent lumbosacral step or short trunk in higher-grade slips
Gait: shortened stride, flexed hips and knees, and antalgic posture in adolescents
Pelvic tilt and standing posture; trunk lean to relieve symptoms
palpation: A palpable step-off at the slipped spinous process (step-deformity palpation) [r13]
Paraspinal tenderness and guarding at the symptomatic level (nonspecific)
Tenderness at the L5 spinous process or pars region
rangeOfMotion: Lumbar flexion and extension: extension is usually painful and flexion relieving
Sustained standing extension for 30–60 seconds to reproduce symptoms (clinical convention)
Hamstring length (straight leg raise) and hip range
Repeated movements and sustained postures to find a symptom-relieving direction
strength: Trunk endurance: side plank, prone hold and extensor endurance (clinical convention)
Single-leg squat and calf raise repetitions to detect S1 weakness
neuro: Dermatomes, reflexes (knee and ankle) and myotomes L2–S1
Straight leg raise and slump for L5 or S1 root irritation
Saddle sensation and bladder, bowel and sexual function screening if any suspicion of cauda equina involvement
Re-test at each visit to detect progression of deficit
functional: Squat and hip hinge control without lumbar extension compensation
Single-leg stance and single-leg squat quality
Sport-specific movements that reproduce symptoms (arching, serving, bowling action)

specialTests.name: Step-deformity palpation (palpable spinous process step)
specialTests.purpose: Detect a palpable slip at the lumbosacral or lumbar level
specialTests.procedure: With the patient prone or standing, palpate the spinous processes from L3 to S1 for a step-off compared with adjacent levels.
specialTests.positive: A palpable step at a spinous process. Based on one low risk-of-bias study in athletes, it may be useful for spondylolisthesis [r13].

specialTests.name: History: pain worse with sitting and walking
specialTests.purpose: Associated history features in athletes with spondylolisthesis
specialTests.procedure: Ask about pain with sitting and walking, and about sleep disturbance from pain.
specialTests.positive: Pain worse with sitting and walking, difficulty falling asleep and waking because of pain each had sensitivity above 75% for spondylolisthesis; the review concluded that no recommendations can be made from history data [r13].
specialTests.sensitivity: Above 75% for each of these history items (athletes)

specialTests.name: One-legged hyperextension (stork) test
specialTests.purpose: Historically used for spondylolysis; not a test for slip
specialTests.procedure: The patient stands on one leg and extends and rotates the lumbar spine toward the standing side.
specialTests.positive: Pain reproduced. The test was not supported for spondylolysis and should not rule it in or out [r13].

specialTests.name: Straight leg raise and slump test
specialTests.purpose: Neural mechanosensitivity of the L5 or S1 root
specialTests.procedure: Supine straight leg raise to the point of reproduction of leg pain, or seated slump with neck flexion and knee extension.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of familiar leg pain that changes with neural loading. No accuracy figures specific to spondylolisthesis were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Neurological examination (myotomes, dermatomes, reflexes)
specialTests.purpose: Identify root compression and track progression
specialTests.procedure: Test L2–S1 myotomes, dermatomes and the knee and ankle reflexes bilaterally.
specialTests.positive: Weakness, sensory loss or reduced reflex in a root distribution. No accuracy figures specific to spondylolisthesis were identified in the sources reviewed.

clinicalRules.name: Slip percentage and slip angle
clinicalRules.description: Grade the slip on a standing lateral radiograph by percentage (Meyerding) [r2]. Higher slip angle was associated with failure of non-surgical treatment in high-grade slips (Level III evidence) [r10].

clinicalRules.name: Cauda equina screen
clinicalRules.description: Ask about saddle sensory change, bladder and bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction and bilateral leg symptoms or weakness. Any positive item is a same-day emergency referral (see the cauda equina syndrome page).

clinicalRules.name: Growing athlete rule
clinicalRules.description: Slip progression tends to occur around the early pubertal growth spurt and early after diagnosis, and the percentage of the initial slip predicts progression, so growing adolescents with higher-percentage slips need serial radiographic monitoring [r5].

outcomeMeasures.name: Oswestry Disability Index (ODI)
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary disability outcome in the SPORT trial and the Swedish fusion trial [r7,r8,r14]

outcomeMeasures.name: SF-36 bodily pain and physical function
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcomes in the SPORT trial for degenerative spondylolisthesis [r7,r8]

outcomeMeasures.name: Disability Rating Index and visual analogue scale for pain
outcomeMeasures.use: Used in the randomised comparison of surgery with an exercise program in isthmic spondylolisthesis [r6]

outcomeMeasures.name: Patient-Specific Functional Scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Individual goals such as returning to a sport, walking distance or sitting tolerance

outcomeMeasures.name: Slip percentage and slip angle on standing lateral radiograph
outcomeMeasures.use: Monitor progression, especially in growing athletes [r5,r10]

imaging.indication: First-line imaging to confirm and grade the slip, and to measure the percentage of slip and, in high-grade slips, the slip angle
imaging.findings: Forward displacement graded by the Meyerding system [r2]; a lytic or elongated pars may be visible on oblique views

imaging.indication: Suspected dynamic instability or before surgical planning
imaging.findings: Change in translation between positions; findings should be interpreted with the clinical picture (clinical convention)

imaging.indication: Characterise the pars defect and bony anatomy
imaging.findings: Bilateral or unilateral pars defects; in a 2000-person CT series, 74.5% of bilateral defects had a slip [r3]

imaging.indication: Neural compression (foraminal or central), radicular or claudicant symptoms, suspected active pars stress reaction, or before surgery
imaging.findings: Foraminal and canal narrowing, root compression, disc degeneration and marrow oedema at an active pars lesion

differentials.name: Spondylolysis (pars stress fracture without slip)
differentials.distinguishing: Extension-provoked back pain in an adolescent athlete with no slip; imaging shows a pars stress reaction or defect without displacement. It may be the earlier stage of an isthmic slip [r3].

differentials.name: Lumbar spinal stenosis
differentials.distinguishing: Older adult, bilateral buttock and leg symptoms on walking relieved by sitting, with or without a degenerative slip [r7].

differentials.name: Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Dermatomal leg pain with positive neural tension and a concordant disc herniation, without a slip.

differentials.name: Lumbar facet joint pain
differentials.distinguishing: Non-dermatomal back and buttock pain without a step or a radiographic slip.

differentials.name: Acute low back pain
differentials.distinguishing: Nonspecific back pain without a slip on imaging; a slip is often an incidental finding.

differentials.name: Cauda equina syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: New bladder, bowel, saddle or sexual dysfunction, or progressive bilateral weakness; an emergency.

differentials.name: Vertebral fracture, infection or malignancy
differentials.distinguishing: Constant or night pain, systemic features, history of cancer, steroid use or trauma; consider traumatic and pathological slips (Wiltse types IV and V) [r1].

redFlags: EMERGENCY: possible cauda equina syndrome. New urinary retention or loss of bladder sensation, faecal incontinence, saddle (perineal) numbness, new sexual dysfunction, or progressive bilateral leg weakness need same-day emergency referral for urgent MRI and surgical review.
Progressive or severe motor deficit (for example a new foot drop): arrange urgent spinal surgical review.

A high-grade slip (Meyerding III–V) or a progressing slip, especially in a growing adolescent: refer to a spinal surgeon, because slip progression is a specific concern in high-grade and dysplastic slips and surgery is commonly recommended [r10].
Constant, night or escalating pain, fever, weight loss, history of cancer or significant trauma: consider traumatic or pathological slip, infection or malignancy and investigate.
Severe or persistent disabling radicular pain or neurogenic claudication not improving with appropriate care: arrange specialist review, as surgery is an option [r7,r8].

management.principles: Most people with a low-grade slip are managed without surgery: education and reassurance (most slips are benign and change little [r4,r5]), activity, and a progressive exercise program. In degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis, guideline-supported multimodal non-surgical care applies [r15]. Refer for surgical opinion when there is a neurological deficit, a high-grade or progressing slip, or persistent disabling symptoms despite adequate non-surgical care [r10]. The surgical evidence is mostly observational: in SPORT, randomised comparisons were limited by high crossover, and as-treated analyses favoured surgery [r7,r8]. Make the decision together, explaining both options and their limits.

medical.name: Bracing (adolescents)
medical.description: The role of bracing in paediatric spondylolisthesis is not well established; evidence is Level III–IV [r10]. Used by some surgeons for symptomatic pars lesions (see the spondylolysis page).

medical.name: Epidural corticosteroid injection (neurogenic claudication)
medical.description: The 2021 guideline for lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication, whose target population includes those with spondylolisthesis, recommended against epidural steroid injection (high-quality evidence) [r15]. Evidence specific to spondylolisthesis is lacking.

medical.name: Decompression with or without fusion (degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis)
medical.description: In SPORT, the intention-to-treat analysis of the randomised cohort (304 patients) showed no significant effects at 2 years or at 3 and 4 years, limited by crossover (about 40% in each direction at 1 year; 66% of the surgical arm and 54% of the non-surgical arm received surgery by 4 years). The as-treated analysis showed a significant advantage for surgery at 2 years (bodily pain 18.1, physical function 18.3, ODI −16.7) and at 4 years (15.3, 18.9 and −14.3) [r7,r8].

medical.name: Fusion added to decompression
medical.description: In a trial of 247 patients with stenosis (135 with degenerative spondylolisthesis), adding fusion to decompression gave no better outcomes than decompression alone at 2 and 5 years, and results were similar with and without spondylolisthesis [r14]. The surgeon's judgement and instability findings guide the choice.

medical.name: Posterolateral fusion for adult isthmic spondylolisthesis
medical.description: In 111 adults aged 18–55 years with at least 1 year of symptoms, fusion gave better function and pain than an exercise program at 1 and 2 years (P < 0.01), although the exercise program was brief and the groups were not blinded [r6]. Transpedicular instrumentation added no benefit in a 77-patient randomised comparison [r16].

medical.name: Surgery for high-grade or dysplastic slips and for children
medical.description: Surgery is commonly recommended to prevent progression in high-grade and dysplastic slips (Level III–IV evidence). Instrumentation with reduction lowers the risk of non-union, and circumferential fusion is superior to posterior-only or anterior-only fusion (Level III) [r10]. In one long-term series, fusion in situ had no significant effect on progression [r5].

physio.name: Education, reassurance and activity advice
physio.description: Explain that most slips are low grade and change little, that pain does not track the slip, and that people with pars defects followed a course like the general population [r4,r5]. Encourage normal activity within symptom limits.

physio.name: Multimodal non-surgical care (education, home exercise, manual therapy and rehabilitation) for degenerative slips with stenosis
physio.description: The 2021 guideline for lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication, which includes people with spondylolisthesis, conditionally recommended multimodal care (moderate-quality evidence) [r15].

physio.name: Specific stabilising exercise (deep abdominal activation with multifidus co-activation)
physio.description: In 44 patients with chronic low back pain and radiological spondylolysis or spondylolisthesis, a 10-week specific exercise program reduced pain and disability, maintained at 30 months, while the control group showed no change. The trial is small and older, with postal follow-up [r12].

physio.name: General strength and conditioning (hip, trunk, leg strength and fitness)
physio.description: Progressive loading of the hip and trunk is standard practice and was a component of successful exercise programs in lumbar stenosis; no spondylolisthesis-specific dose trial was identified. Dosages are clinical convention.

physio.name: Blanket sport restriction for limited low-grade slips
physio.description: In 86 young athletes with spondylolysis or spondylolisthesis, displacement increased in 33 but all remained asymptomatic during training, and the authors saw no justification for generally advising against competitive sports in limited slips [r11]. Symptomatic athletes with an active pars lesion need modification (see the spondylolysis page).

physio.name: Serial radiographic monitoring of growing adolescents
physio.description: Slips tend to progress at the early pubertal growth spurt and the percentage of the initial slip predicts progression, so growing adolescents need follow-up radiographs [r5].

physio.name: Forceful end-range extension or rotation mobilisation or manipulation at the slipped level
physio.description: Avoid forceful passive end-range techniques at a symptomatic unstable level (clinical convention). Gentle mobilisation of adjacent segments may help symptoms.

education: A slip of the spine is common and usually stable. Most slips are low grade, they change little over a lifetime, and many people have no pain at all.
A scan does not show how much pain you have. People with the same slip can have very different symptoms.
Exercise to strengthen the deep trunk and hip muscles is the foundation of treatment, and you do not need to avoid all activity or sport for a low-grade slip.
If you are still growing, your physio and doctor will check the slip with an X-ray from time to time, particularly around growth spurts.
Surgery is an option if pain or nerve symptoms stay disabling after good non-surgical care. It helps some people more than others, and the decision is yours.
Go to an emergency department the same day if you notice numbness around the genitals or buttocks, difficulty passing urine, loss of bowel control, or leg weakness that is getting worse.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and symptom-led. The exercise evidence is limited to a 10-week specific stabilising program in chronic spondylolysis or spondylolisthesis [r12] and the multimodal approach in spinal stenosis [r15], so dosages below are clinical convention. Start with education, symptom-relieving positions and walking, then deep segmental control with multifidus co-activation, then hip, trunk and leg strength, then sport- or job-specific loading. Avoid repeated end-range lumbar extension and rotation under load while symptoms are irritable (clinical convention). Growing adolescents need monitoring around the growth spurt [r5].

stages.name: Settle & educate
goals: Understand the diagnosis and its generally benign course
Pain settling and daily activities tolerated
Identify the positions and movements that relieve or provoke symptoms
precautions: Refer the same day for any new bladder, bowel or saddle symptoms or progressing weakness
Avoid repeated end-range extension and loaded rotation while symptoms are irritable (clinical convention)
In a growing adolescent with a high-percentage slip, confirm monitoring and specialist input before progressing

exercises.name: Walking program
exercises.dosage: 10–30 minutes, daily, as symptoms allow (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Walk tall and relaxed; stop before symptoms build

exercises.name: Supine knee to chest
exercises.dosage: 3 holds of 20–30 seconds per leg, twice daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Relax into the floor; posterior pelvic tilt

exercises.name: Cat–camel in comfortable range
exercises.dosage: 2 sets of 10 slow repetitions, 2–3 times daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Smooth, pain-free range

exercises.name: Hamstring and hip mobility (for example supine heel slide, then gentle hamstring stretch)
exercises.dosage: 2–3 holds of 30 seconds per side, daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis neutral; no pain at the slip

exercises.name: Deep abdominal activation in supine (drawing in)
exercises.dosage: 10 repetitions of 10-second holds, twice daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Gentle co-contraction, continue breathing

progressionCriteria: Resting pain 4/10 or less and sleep not routinely disturbed
Understands what to avoid and what to do for a flare

stages.name: Segmental control
goals: Deep abdominal activation with multifidus co-activation in static postures and functional tasks
precautions: Progress a new demand only if symptoms are 2/10 or lower and settle by the next day (clinical convention)
Keep the spine neutral; avoid arching under load

exercises.name: Deep abdominal activation with multifidus co-activation in aggravating postures
exercises.dosage: Daily, integrated into previously aggravating postures and tasks; the trial program ran 10 weeks [r12]
exercises.cues: Gentle co-contraction; avoid bracing or breath-holding

exercises.name: Dead bug (neutral spine)
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8 repetitions per side, daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Low back flat as the limbs move

exercises.name: Bird-dog
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8 repetitions per side with 5-second holds (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Reach long; keep the pelvis level; avoid arching

exercises.name: Glute bridge
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 10 repetitions with a 3-second hold (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels; posterior pelvic tilt at the top

exercises.name: Side plank (knees, then feet)
exercises.dosage: 3 holds of 15–30 seconds per side, building to 45 seconds (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Stack the hips; lift the waist away from the floor

progressionCriteria: Maintains deep abdominal co-contraction through the exercises above without compensation
Pain 2/10 or less during exercises and daily tasks
Side plank at least 30 seconds each side (clinical convention)

stages.name: Build strength & power
goals: Hip hinge and squat patterns without lumbar extension compensation
Low-level impact tolerance if needed for sport
precautions: Increase load or volume by about 5–10% a week, one variable at a time (clinical convention)
Stop and review if leg symptoms or extension-provoked pain return

exercises.name: Hip thrust
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8–10 repetitions at a load leaving 2–3 in reserve, 2–3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Tuck the pelvis at the top; ribs down

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 6–8 repetitions, progressive load, 2 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Hinge from the hips; keep the bar close; spine neutral

exercises.name: Single-leg bridge
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8 repetitions per leg, 3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level; avoid arching

exercises.name: Squat
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8–10 repetitions, 2–3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Knees follow the toes; chest up; neutral spine

exercises.name: Forearm plank
exercises.dosage: 3 holds of 30–45 seconds, 3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Straight line from head to heels; squeeze the glutes

progressionCriteria: No leg symptoms or extension-provoked pain with loaded exercises
Plank at least 45 seconds and side plank symmetry within about 10% (clinical convention)
Hip hinge and squat with a neutral spine at a meaningful load

stages.name: Return to sport & work
goals: Meet the physical demands of sport or work
Graded exposure to the sport's extension and rotation demands
precautions: Build sport-specific extension and rotation volume gradually: for example start at 25–50% of usual and add about 10–20% a week (clinical convention)
Adolescents: keep radiographic monitoring around growth spurts [r5]
Step back one level if symptoms return

exercises.name: Single-leg squat
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 6–8 repetitions per leg (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Control the knee and pelvis; avoid trunk extension

exercises.name: Farmer carry
exercises.dosage: 3 carries of 20–30 metres at a challenging load, 2 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Walk tall; avoid leaning to the loaded side

exercises.name: Hop and landing progressions
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 6–8 repetitions per leg (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Control the trunk on landing

exercises.name: Sport-specific technique drills at reduced intensity
exercises.dosage: Start at 25–50% of usual volume and increase weekly (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Quality over volume; coach involvement is helpful

exercises.name: Graded floor-to-waist lift (work)
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 5–8 repetitions, starting at half the work load and increasing weekly (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Load close to the body; neutral spine

progressionCriteria: Full training or duties completed without symptoms
Self-management plan agreed; monitoring plan agreed for growing athletes

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria for spondylolisthesis were identified in the sources reviewed; the following reflect clinical convention
Low-grade, stable slip with no neurological deficit; high-grade slips need specialist clearance
Pain-free daily activities and sport-specific training at full intensity, with no pain the following day
Deep trunk and hip strength and endurance adequate for the sport, with side-to-side symmetry within about 10%
Pain-free lumbar extension and sport-specific extension and rotation movements
A monitoring plan in growing athletes, with radiographic follow-up around the growth spurt [r5]
tests: Side plank and prone extensor endurance, both sides
Repeat sustained extension and sport-specific movement provocation without pain
Oswestry Disability Index or Patient-Specific Functional Scale against the person's goal

prognosis: Low-grade isthmic slips usually behave well. In a 45-year prospective study unselected for pain, subjects with unilateral defects never slipped, slip progression slowed with each decade, there was no association between slip progression and low back pain, SF-36 scores matched the general population and no subject reached a 40% slip [r4]. In 272 children and adolescents followed for a mean 14.8 years, 90% of the slip had already occurred at the first examination, more than 10% progression occurred in 62 patients mostly within a year of the first examination or surgery, fusion in situ had no significant effect on progression and the only predictor was the percentage of primary slip [r5]. In 86 young athletes, displacement increased in 33 (average 10.5%), did not progress in 36 and decreased in 7, and all remained asymptomatic over 4.8 years [r11]. Studies suggest a benign course for low-grade (<50%) slips but many patients still present with pain, and slip progression is a specific concern in high-grade and dysplastic slips [r10]. In degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis, as-treated surgical patients had greater improvement in pain and function than non-surgical patients, maintained at 4 years, although the randomised comparisons were limited by crossover [r7,r8]. In adults with isthmic slips, fusion gave better function and pain than an exercise program at 2 years [r6], while a 10-week specific exercise program reduced pain and disability, maintained at 30 months, in chronic spondylolysis or spondylolisthesis [r12].
prevention: No intervention has been shown to prevent spondylolisthesis; the points below are clinical convention.
Manage training load in extension-and-rotation sports and take persistent extension-provoked back pain in an adolescent athlete seriously (see the spondylolysis page).
Monitor known slips in growing adolescents around the growth spurt [r5].
In adults, maintain general fitness and hip and trunk strength; no evidence was identified that exercise prevents degenerative slip.
clinicalPearls: Slip percentage guides the plan. Most low-grade slips change little, and in a long-term series 90% of the slip had occurred by the first examination, so do not catastrophise a low-grade finding [r5].
Treat the person, not the radiograph. Pain did not track slip progression and people with pars defects had SF-36 scores like the general population [r4].
Palpate for the step. Step-deformity palpation had 60–88% sensitivity and 87–100% specificity in one low-risk-of-bias study of athletes, and the one-legged hyperextension test is not supported [r13].

A blanket sport ban is not justified for limited slips. In 86 young athletes with displacement progressing in 33, all stayed asymptomatic [r11], but high-grade slips and symptomatic active lesions need specialist input.

Be honest about surgery. The randomised comparisons were limited by crossover, as-treated analyses favoured surgery for degenerative slips with stenosis, and fusion added to decompression was no better in a trial that included degenerative spondylolisthesis [r7,r8,r14].
Do not forget the cauda equina. A slip with stenosis can compress the canal; ask every patient about bladder, bowel and saddle sensation and refer the same day if positive.

captions.text: A young athlete trains many times a week in a sport that arches and twists the lower back.
Repeated extension and rotation load the pars interarticularis of L5.
Microdamage builds faster than the growing skeleton repairs it.
If the pars fails on both sides, nothing holds the L5 body back against forward shear.
Back pain starts, often with hamstring tightness. Many slips cause no symptoms at all.
Zooming into the lumbosacral spine, seen from the side, with the L5 pars in view.
L5 sits on the sloping top of the sacrum, held by the disc in front and the facet joints behind.
Upright posture and extension load the L5 pars with anterior shear.
A stress fracture through the pars, on both sides, leaves the body disconnected from its arch.
The disc below loses height as the slip develops.
The L5 body slides forward on S1. Most of the slip happens early, around the growth spurt.
In some people the L5 root is pinched in the foramen, giving leg pain.
In older adults the slip is degenerative, usually L4–5, with no pars defect.
Healthy pars bone: trabeculae and cortex in balance.
Repetitive extension and rotation strain the bone cyclically.
Microcracks accumulate in the cortex and trabeculae.
Resorption outpaces new bone formation, weakening the pars.
A stress reaction develops, with marrow oedema on MRI.
A stress fracture forms. If it fails to unite, the gap persists and allows the slip.
